name: Binary relation
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs
quick: A selection of ordered pairs describing which first inputs relate to which second inputs.
definition: A binary relation from $A$ to $B$ is a subset of $A\times B$. The notation $aRb$ means $(a,b)\in R$. A relation on $A$ uses $A$ for both input positions.
example: For users Ada and Bo, the pairs (Ada, read), (Ada, write), and (Bo, read) record three permissions.
confusion: A general relation can give an input no outputs or several outputs; it is not necessarily a function.

name: Matrix
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs
quick: A rectangular table of entries arranged in rows and columns.
definition: Row and column labels identify each entry. A finite relation matrix places 1 at row a and column b when aRb, and 0 otherwise. State the row and column order.
example: For R = {(a,b)} on {a,b}, in that order the rows are (0,1) and (0,0).
confusion: Swapping row and column roles reverses the relation.

name: Boolean matrix
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs
quick: A matrix whose entries are only 0 and 1.
definition: For a finite relation, 1 records a present ordered pair and 0 records an absent pair. These values encode truth of membership.
example: With R = {(a,a),(a,b)} on {a,b}, its rows in order a,b are (1,1) and (0,0).
confusion: An entry of 0 is an explicit absence, not an unknown value.

name: Main diagonal
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs
quick: Entries whose row and column have the same position in a square matrix.
definition: For a relation on one set, use the same row and column order. The main-diagonal entries then test whether each object relates to itself.
example: In a relation matrix with row/column order a,b,c, inspect entries (a,a), (b,b), and (c,c).
confusion: A diagonal of a drawn graph is a different geometric idea; here the term refers to matrix positions.

name: Reflexive relation
quick: Every object in the underlying set relates to itself.
definition: A relation R on A is reflexive when $\forall a\in A,\ aRa$. In a relation drawing every vertex needs a loop.
example: Equality is reflexive; each integer equals itself.
confusion: A missing loop at even one object defeats reflexivity. The underlying set must be stated.

name: Symmetric relation
quick: Every related pair has its reverse.
definition: A relation is symmetric when $aRb$ implies $bRa$ for every a,b in its underlying set. The condition does not require pairs to exist.
example: Having the same birthday month is symmetric: swapping two people preserves whether their months match.
confusion: Not symmetric does not mean antisymmetric. Test the two definitions separately.

name: Antisymmetric relation
quick: Distinct objects cannot relate in both directions.
definition: For all a,b, if aRb and bRa, then a=b. Loops are permitted; mutual relatedness is forbidden only for distinct objects.
example: Numerical $\leq$ is antisymmetric: a≤b and b≤a force equality.
confusion: This is not the same as forbidding every reverse arrow, which is asymmetry.

name: Transitive relation
quick: Every two-step connection has its direct connection.
definition: For all a,b,c, aRb and bRc imply aRc. Inputs may repeat: aRb and bRa require loops at both objects.
example: For numbers, a≤b and b≤c imply a≤c.
confusion: Checking only three distinct inputs misses failures involving repeated objects.

name: Irreflexive relation
quick: No object relates to itself.
definition: R is irreflexive when $\forall a,\neg aRa$: every loop is absent.
example: Strict numerical comparison < is irreflexive because no number is strictly less than itself.
confusion: Not reflexive requires only one missing loop; irreflexive requires all loops to be missing.

name: Asymmetric relation
quick: A related pair never has its reverse, even when both inputs are the same.
definition: For every a,b, aRb implies not bRa. This forbids both two-way connections between distinct objects and loops.
example: Strict numerical comparison < is asymmetric.
confusion: Antisymmetry permits loops; asymmetry does not.

name: Equivalence relation
quick: A relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
definition: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. These properties make a chosen sense of sameness consistent: every object matches itself, matches can be reversed, and two successive matches give a match between the endpoints. Its equivalence classes partition the underlying set.
example: Integers having the same remainder when divided by 3 form an equivalence relation.
confusion: Sharing a friend need not be transitive; a resemblance relation is not automatically an equivalence relation.

name: Divisibility
quick: One integer is an integer multiple of another.
definition: For integers d and n, $d\mid n$ means $n=dk$ for some integer k. This definition permits negative multipliers and gives $0\mid0$, while 0 divides no nonzero integer.
example: $3\mid12$ because $12=3\cdot4$. Also $3\mid-6$ because $-6=3(-2)$.
confusion: The notation d|n is not the fraction d/n. It asks whether an integer multiplier exists.

name: Modulus in congruence
quick: The fixed positive integer that determines the congruence classes.
definition: For modulus m, two integers are congruent when their difference is divisible by m. Standard remainders range from 0 to m−1.
example: With modulus 3, 1 and 4 are congruent because their difference is a multiple of 3.
confusion: The modulus stays fixed throughout a congruence claim. This use is different from absolute value or magnitude.

name: Congruence modulo an integer
quick: Equality of remainders for a fixed positive modulus.
definition: For positive integer m, $a\equiv b\pmod m$ means $m\mid(a-b)$. This is an equivalence relation on the integers.
example: $1\equiv4\pmod3$ and $-2\equiv1\pmod3$: both differences are multiples of 3.
confusion: Here ≡ relates integers modulo m; it is not the logical-equivalence notation from the logic lesson.

name: String
quick: A finite ordered sequence of symbols.
definition: Its length counts symbols, including repetitions. A binary string permits only the symbols 0 and 1.
example: The binary strings 01 and 10 differ, but both have length two.
confusion: Leading zeroes matter in strings; 01 is a two-symbol string, not just another way to write the number 1.

name: Binary string
quick: A finite string made only of the symbols 0 and 1.
definition: Position and repetition matter. At length two the complete list is 00, 01, 10, and 11.
example: Under the relation “has the same length,” the class of 01 contains all four length-two binary strings.
confusion: A string of bits is not a set of its symbols: 001 and 01 are different strings.

name: Equivalence class
quick: All objects equivalent to a chosen object under a stated equivalence relation.
definition: For R on A, $[a]=\{x\in A:xRa\}$. Any member can name the class. Distinct classes are disjoint, and the classes cover A.
confusion: Equal classes need not have equal representative labels.

name: Representative of a class
quick: A chosen member used to name its equivalence class.
definition: The notation [a] uses a as a representative of all objects related to it. Choosing a different member of the class names the same set.
example: Modulo 3, either 1 or 4 can represent the class of integers with remainder 1.
confusion: The representative is one object; the class is the set containing all equivalent objects.

name: Partial order
quick: A relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
definition: A partial order on a set is a reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive relation. With $\preceq$ denoting this relation, each $a\preceq a$ holds; $a\preceq b$ and $b\preceq a$ force $a=b$; and $a\preceq b$ and $b\preceq c$ imply $a\preceq c$. Distinct elements need not be comparable in either direction.
example: Subset inclusion orders a power set, but {1} and {2} need not be comparable.
confusion: Antisymmetry does not require that every pair be comparable.

name: Partially ordered set
quick: A set together with a specified partial order.
definition: The abbreviation poset names the combination of objects and their comparison relation. The same objects can carry different orders.
example: The subsets of {1,2}, ordered by inclusion, form a four-element poset.
confusion: The underlying set alone does not tell you what below or above means.

name: Comparable elements
quick: Two elements for which at least one direction of the order holds.
definition: In a partial order, a and b are comparable if a≼b or b≼a. Otherwise they are incomparable.
example: Under subset inclusion, {1} and {1,2} are comparable; {1} and {2} are incomparable.
confusion: Different elements may be incomparable. Equal elements are comparable by reflexivity.

name: Total order
quick: A partial order in which every pair of elements is comparable.
definition: In addition to the partial-order axioms, for every a,b require a≼b or b≼a.
example: Ordinary ≤ on the integers is total.
confusion: Total does not mean finite or bounded; the integers have a total order but no greatest integer.

name: Hasse diagram
quick: A drawing of the cover comparisons in a finite partial order, read upward.
definition: Draw larger elements above smaller ones and join a to b when b covers a. Omit loops, arrowheads, and comparisons implied by longer upward paths. Equality and upward paths recover all comparisons.
example: For the power set of {1,2}, the four cover joins form a diamond from ∅ to {1,2}.
confusion: A missing direct join does not imply incomparability; an upward path may supply the comparison.

name: Cover in a partial order
quick: An immediate strict comparison with no element strictly between its endpoints.
definition: In a partially ordered set, $b$ covers $a$ when $a\prec b$ and there is no element $c$ in the set with $a\prec c\prec b$. Here $a\prec b$ means both $a\preceq b$ and $a\ne b$. Thus a cover is an immediate strict comparison within the specified set.
example: Under subset inclusion on $\mathcal P(\{1,2\})$, the set $\{1\}$ covers $\varnothing$. The set $\{1,2\}$ does not cover $\varnothing$, because $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ are intermediate elements.
confusion: Cover depends on which objects are in the poset. An intermediate value outside it does not count.

name: Least element
quick: An element below every element of the poset.
definition: a is least when a≼x for every x, including a itself. Antisymmetry ensures at most one least element.
example: Under divisibility on {1,2,3,6}, 1 is least because it divides every element.
confusion: Minimal does not mean least; several incomparable elements can be minimal.

name: Minimal element
quick: An element with no strictly smaller element in the poset.
definition: a is minimal when there is no x with x≺a. There may be several incomparable minimal elements.
example: Under divisibility on {2,3,6}, 2 and 3 are minimal but neither is least.
confusion: Minimal says nothing about elements incomparable with a.

name: Greatest element
quick: An element above every element of the poset.
definition: a is greatest when x≼a for every x. Antisymmetry ensures at most one greatest element.
example: Under divisibility on {2,3,6}, 6 is greatest.
confusion: Greatest does not mean largest numerical value unless the chosen order makes that comparison.

name: Maximal element
quick: An element with no strictly larger element in the poset.
definition: a is maximal when there is no x with a≺x. Distinct maximal elements can be incomparable.
example: Under divisibility on {1,2,3}, 2 and 3 are maximal; neither is greatest.
confusion: A maximal element need not be above all the other elements.

name: Inverse relation
quick: The relation obtained by reversing every ordered pair.
definition: If R is a relation from A to B, its inverse $R^{-1}$ is a relation from B to A with (b,a) present exactly when (a,b) is in R.
example: The inverse of {(1,a),(2,a)} is {(a,1),(a,2)}.
confusion: The superscript −1 does not mean reciprocal here. An inverse relation may give several outputs to one input.

name: Composition of relations
quick: Following one relation and then a second through a matching intermediate object.
definition: For R from A to B and S from B to C, $S\circ R$ contains (a,c) exactly when some b in B satisfies aRb and bSc. Read from right to left: first R, then S.
example: From R={(1,a),(1,b)} and S={(a,u),(b,u)}, the composition is {(1,u)}.
confusion: Two different witnesses for the same final pair still produce only one member. Composition order matters.

name: Transitive closure
quick: The smallest transitive relation containing the original relation.
definition: It adds exactly pairs connected by one or more steps in the original relation. On a finite set, repeatedly adding missing two-step shortcuts eventually stabilizes.
example: Starting from {(a,b),(b,c)}, add (a,c).
confusion: Zero-step self-connections are not included automatically; cycles may still force loops.

name: Reflexive-transitive closure
quick: The smallest relation containing the original that is both reflexive and transitive.
definition: It records reachability by zero or more steps, so every element has a loop even when it has no connections to other objects.
example: On {a,b,c}, the closure of {(a,b)} is {(a,a),(b,b),(c,c),(a,b)}.
confusion: Remember the underlying set; isolated elements still need loops.

name: Reflexive closure
section: Building closures without losing the meaning
quick: The smallest reflexive relation containing the original relation.
definition: Add every missing pair (a,a) for objects a in the underlying set, keeping every original pair.
example: On {a,b}, the reflexive closure of {(a,b)} is {(a,a),(b,b),(a,b)}.
confusion: It adds loops, not missing reverse pairs or transitive shortcuts.

name: Symmetric closure
section: Building closures without losing the meaning
quick: The smallest symmetric relation containing the original relation.
definition: Keep every original pair and add its reverse when missing; equivalently take the union of R and its inverse.
example: The symmetric closure of {(a,b),(b,c)} adds (b,a) and (c,b).
confusion: It need not become transitive or reflexive.

name: aRb — a is related to b
section: Relations as sets of ordered pairs
quick: A selection of ordered pairs describing which first inputs relate to which second inputs.
definition: A binary relation from $A$ to $B$ is a subset of $A\times B$. The notation $aRb$ means $(a,b)\in R$. A relation on $A$ uses $A$ for both input positions.
example: For users Ada and Bo, the pairs (Ada, read), (Ada, write), and (Bo, read) record three permissions.
confusion: A general relation can give an input no outputs or several outputs; it is not necessarily a function.

name: ∣ — divides
quick: One integer is an integer multiple of another.
definition: For integers d and n, $d\mid n$ means $n=dk$ for some integer k. This definition permits negative multipliers and gives $0\mid0$, while 0 divides no nonzero integer.
example: $3\mid12$ because $12=3\cdot4$. Also $3\mid-6$ because $-6=3(-2)$.
confusion: The notation d|n is not the fraction d/n. It asks whether an integer multiplier exists.

name: ≡ (mod m) — congruence
quick: Equality of remainders for a fixed positive modulus.
definition: For positive integer m, $a\equiv b\pmod m$ means $m\mid(a-b)$. This is an equivalence relation on the integers.
example: $1\equiv4\pmod3$ and $-2\equiv1\pmod3$: both differences are multiples of 3.
confusion: Here ≡ relates integers modulo m; it is not the logical-equivalence notation from the logic lesson.

name: [a] — equivalence class
quick: All objects equivalent to a chosen object under a stated equivalence relation.
definition: For R on A, $[a]=\{x\in A:xRa\}$. Any member can name the class. Distinct classes are disjoint, and the classes cover A.
confusion: Equal classes need not have equal representative labels.

name: ≼ — partial-order comparison
quick: A relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
definition: A partial order on a set is a reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive relation. With $\preceq$ denoting this relation, each $a\preceq a$ holds; $a\preceq b$ and $b\preceq a$ force $a=b$; and $a\preceq b$ and $b\preceq c$ imply $a\preceq c$. Distinct elements need not be comparable in either direction.
example: Subset inclusion orders a power set, but {1} and {2} need not be comparable.
confusion: Antisymmetry does not require that every pair be comparable.

name: ≺ — strict comparison
quick: $a\prec b$ means that $a$ is below $b$ in the specified order and is unequal to $b$.
definition: Given a partial order $\preceq$, define $a\prec b$ to mean $a\preceq b$ and $a\ne b$. Read it as “a is strictly below b.” This comparison excludes equality but can include comparisons through intermediate elements.
example: Under subset inclusion on $\mathcal P(\{1,2\})$, $\varnothing\prec\{1,2\}$. This strict comparison holds even though $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ are intermediate elements.
confusion: Strict comparison is not the same as a cover: a cover additionally rules out intermediate elements.

name: R⁻¹ — inverse relation
quick: The relation obtained by reversing every ordered pair.
definition: If R is a relation from A to B, its inverse $R^{-1}$ is a relation from B to A with (b,a) present exactly when (a,b) is in R.
example: The inverse of {(1,a),(2,a)} is {(a,1),(a,2)}.
confusion: The superscript −1 does not mean reciprocal here. An inverse relation may give several outputs to one input.

name: ∘ — relation composition
quick: Following one relation and then a second through a matching intermediate object.
definition: For R from A to B and S from B to C, $S\circ R$ contains (a,c) exactly when some b in B satisfies aRb and bSc. Read from right to left: first R, then S.
example: From R={(1,a),(1,b)} and S={(a,u),(b,u)}, the composition is {(1,u)}.
confusion: Two different witnesses for the same final pair still produce only one member. Composition order matters.
